## Proof

Let $\gamma, \eta : [a,b] \to C$ be two homeomorphisms. Define $h = \gamma^{-1}\circ \eta : [a,b]\to[a,b]$. Since $\gamma,\eta$ are homeomorphisms, $h$ is a homeomorphism of $[a,b]$ onto itself.

**Claim.** $h$ is either strictly increasing or strictly decreasing.

*Proof of claim.* $h$ is continuous and injective on the interval $[a,b]$. A continuous injective function on an interval is strictly monotone (standard result). Since $h$ is a bijection onto $[a,b]$, if $h$ is increasing then $h(a)=a,\ h(b)=b$; if decreasing then $h(a)=b,\ h(b)=a$. $\square$

The length of a curve $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is
$$L(\varphi)=\sup_{P}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\rho\big(\varphi(t_i),\varphi(t_{i+1})\big),$$
where the supremum ranges over all partitions $P=\{a=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_n=b\}$.

**Case 1: $h$ strictly increasing.** Then $\eta=\gamma\circ h$ with $h(a)=a,\ h(b)=b$. For any partition $P=\{t_0<\dots<t_n\}$, the image $h(P)=\{h(t_0)<\dots<h(t_n)\}$ is again a partition of $[a,b]$. Conversely, every partition $Q$ of $[a,b]$ equals $h(P)$ for $P=h^{-1}(Q)$. Hence the map $P\mapsto h(P)$ is a bijection on the set of all partitions, and
$$\sum_i \rho(\eta(t_i),\eta(t_{i+1}))=\sum_i \rho(\gamma(h(t_i)),\gamma(h(t_{i+1}))).$$
Taking the supremum over $P$ is the same as taking it over $h(P)$, so $L(\eta)=L(\gamma)$.

**Case 2: $h$ strictly decreasing.** Then $h(a)=b,\ h(b)=a$. For a partition $P=\{a=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_n=b\}$, the values $h(t_0)>h(t_1)>\dots>h(t_n)$, i.e. $b=h(t_0)>h(t_1)>\dots>h(t_n)=a$. Set $s_i:=h(t_{n-i})$, giving a partition $Q=\{a=s_0<s_1<\dots<s_n=b\}$. Then
$$\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\rho\big(\gamma(h(t_i)),\gamma(h(t_{i+1}))\big)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\rho\big(\gamma(s_{n-i}),\gamma(s_{n-i-1})\big)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\rho\big(\gamma(s_j),\gamma(s_{j+1})\big),$$
(substituting $j=n-i-1$), which is the sum for $\gamma$ over $Q$. The correspondence $P\mapsto Q$ is a bijection on partitions (it is the composition of reversal with the decreasing bijection $h$), so again $L(\eta)=L(\gamma)$.

In both cases $L(\eta)=L(\gamma)$. Since $\gamma,\eta$ were arbitrary homeomorphisms $[a,b]\to C$, **all such parametrizations have the same length**. In particular, if any one parametrization has finite length, every parametrization does, and they all share that same finite value. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE

(Standard result: a continuous injective function on an interval is strictly monotone.) Since h is a bijection, it's injective, hence strictly monotone. L(φ) = sup_P Σ_{i=0}^{n-1} ρ(φ(t_i), φ(t_{i+1}))
where the supremum is over all partitions P = {a = t_0 < t_1 < ... < t_n = b}.

Case 1: h strictly increasing. Then η = γ ∘ h. For any partition P = {t_0 < ... < t_n} of [a,b], the image h(P) = {h(t_0) < ... < h(t_n)} is a partition of [a,b] (since h is increasing bijection with h(a)=a, h(b)=b). Conversely, every partition Q of [a,b] is h(P) for some partition P (namely P = h^{-1}(Q)). Thus:
Σ ρ(η(t_i), η(t_{i+1})) = Σ ρ(γ(h(t_i)), γ(h(t_{i+1})))
and as P ranges over all partitions, h(P) ranges over all partitions. Therefore L(η) = L(γ).

Σ_{i=0}^{n-1} ρ(γ(h(t_i)), γ(h(t_{i+1}))) = Σ_{i=0}^{n-1} ρ(γ(s_{n-i}), γ(s_{n-i-1})) = Σ_{j=0}^{n-1} ρ(γ(s_j), γ(s_{j+1}))
(substituting j = n-i-1). This is the sum for γ over partition Q. As P ranges over all partitions, Q ranges over all partitions (the map P → Q is a bijection on the set of partitions, since it's just reversing and applying h). Therefore L(η) = L(γ).

In both cases, L(η) = L(γ). Since γ and η were arbitrary homeomorphisms, all parametrizations have the same length. In particular, if any one has finite length, all do, and they share that same finite value.
